title.title: The primes are not a sumset
title.subtitle: Claim: no finite modification of the primes equals $A + B$ with $|A|, |B| \ge 2$

panels.caption: the primes $\mathcal{P}$: is some finite change of them a sumset $A + B$?

lines.tex: A + B = \{\, a + b : a \in A,\ b \in B \,\}

beats.text: Ostmann (1956): are the primes, up to finitely many changes, a sumset $A + B$?
Sieves forced any such $A$ and $B$ to have about $\sqrt{x}$ elements below $x$
The claim: no such pair exists

plain: Could the primes be built by adding every number in one list to every number in another? No

steps: Suppose the primes, give or take a few, were all sums $a + b$
Sieves force $A$ and $B$ to look small modulo every prime
A new inverse theorem says such sets can't exist

voice.text: Could the primes, give or take a few, be all the sums from two sets?
If so, both sets look sparse mod every prime, which a new theorem forbids.
